**The Drawer of Unknown Objects**

Every house has one: a drawer, a jar, a shoebox full of objects that have outlived their explanations. Three keys to doors that no longer exist—or never did. A cable compatible with nothing in the visible universe. A single screw, waiting like a monk. Batteries of unknown charge and dubious provenance. The people who own these things cannot throw them away, and cannot say why. But there is a superstition at work, older than any religion still practiced: the belief that the moment you discard the screw, the thing it fits will reveal itself, desperate and incomplete.

So the drawer grows. It becomes an archive of abandoned contexts. Each object was once part of a system—a lamp, a toy, a machine with a manual. The systems are gone now, but the objects persist, orphaned yet still employed.

We call humans pattern-seekers, meaning-makers. But maybe we are also context-keepers. We cannot bear for anything to be fully cut loose from its story. The keys might open something. The cable might charge something. To throw them away would be a small act of demolition—not of the objects, but of possibility itself.

Maybe that is why we keep the other things: ticket stubs, birthday cards, the voicemail we can't bring ourselves to delete. Not because we will need them. Because somewhere in each of us is a librarian who refuses to let a single book go missing, who insists that everything is still on the map, still belongs to something.
